questions.question_text: Simplify $\cos^{2}4x - \sin^{2}4x$ as a single trigonometric ratio.

options.why: Used sine instead of cosine in $\cos^{2}A - \sin^{2}A = \cos 2A$.
Confused the difference $\cos^{2}4x - \sin^{2}4x$ with the Pythagorean sum $\cos^{2}4x + \sin^{2}4x = 1$.
Used the cosine double angle identity but did not double the angle $4x$.

questions.question_text: Simplify $1 - 2\sin^{2}3x$ as a single trigonometric ratio.

options.why: Reversed the subtraction and simplified $2\sin^{2}3x - 1$ instead.
Used sine instead of cosine in $1 - 2\sin^{2}A = \cos 2A$.
Used the cosine double angle identity but did not double the angle $3x$.
Used the denominator $2\sin 2x$ instead of $4\sin 2x$ when simplifying.
Incorrectly expanded $\sin 4x$ as $2\sin^{2}2x$, then divided by $4\sin 2x$.
Forgot the multiplier 2 from the double angle identity in the numerator.
Omitted the factor of 3 when factoring $3(2\cos^2 x - 1)$.
Did not divide 6 by 2 when matching to $2\cos^2 x - 1$.
Confused the cosine double angle identity with the sine double angle identity.

questions.question_text: Which expression is equivalent to $\frac{\sin 2\theta}{\cos\theta}$ for $\cos\theta \neq 0$?

options.why: Forgot the coefficient $2$ in the expansion $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
Multiplied by an extra factor of $2$ instead of cancelling $\cos\theta$.
Divided by $2$ instead of multiplying by $2$ in the double angle numerator.

questions.question_text: Simplify $4\sin 3x\cos 3x$ as a single trigonometric term.

options.why: Doubled the angle correctly but kept the outside coefficient $4$ instead of writing $4\sin 3x\cos 3x = 2(2\sin 3x\cos 3x)$.
Halved the coefficient correctly but left the angle as $3x$, forgetting that $2\sin 3x\cos 3x = \sin 6x$.
Made both slips at once: kept the coefficient $4$ and did not double the angle $3x$.

questions.question_text: Simplify $\frac{1 - \cos 6\theta}{1 + \cos 6\theta}$ to a single trigonometric function of $3\theta$, for $\cos 3\theta \ne 0$.

options.why: Inverted the simplified fraction $\sin^{2}3\theta/\cos^{2}3\theta$.
Dropped both squares when simplifying $\sin^{2}3\theta/\cos^{2}3\theta$.
Omitted the factor $2$ from the denominator $1 + \cos 6\theta = 2\cos^{2}3\theta$.
Inverted the simplified fraction $\cos x/\sin x$ to obtain $\sin x/\cos x = \tan x$.
After simplifying to $\cos x/\sin x$, incorrectly replaced $\cos x$ by $1$.
Incorrectly replaced the denominator $1 - \cos 2x$ by $2\sin x$, then cancelled it from $2\sin x\cos x$.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{\sin 2x}{1 - \cos 2x}$
$= \frac{2\sin x\cos x}{1 - (1 - 2\sin^{2}x)}$
$= \frac{2\sin x\cos x}{2\sin^{2}x}$
$= \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$
$= \cot x$

options.why: Reversed the subtraction and simplified $\frac{1}{2} - \cos^{2}2x$ instead.
Omitted the outside factor $\frac{1}{2}$ from $\frac{1}{2}(2\cos^{2}2x - 1)$.
Kept the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ but did not double the angle $2x$.
Omitted the factor $3$ from the denominator when cancelling $\sin 3\theta$.
Forgot the factor $2$ in $\sin 6\theta = 2\sin 3\theta\cos 3\theta$.
Incorrectly expanded $\sin 6\theta$ as $2\sin^{2}3\theta$, then divided by $3\sin 3\theta$.
